{{Short description|Concept in astrophysics}}
{{More citations needed|date=February 2025}}
The '''free-fall time''' is the characteristic [[time]] that would take a body to collapse under its own [[gravity|gravitational attraction]], if no other forces existed to oppose the collapse. As such, it plays a fundamental role in setting the timescale for a wide variety of astrophysical processes—from [[star formation]] to [[helioseismology|helio-seismology]] to [[supernova]]e—in which gravity plays a dominant role.

==Derivation==

===Infall to a point source of gravity===
It is relatively simple to derive the free-fall time by applying [[Kepler's laws of planetary motion|Kepler's Third Law]] of planetary motion to a [[Elliptic orbit|degenerate elliptic orbit]]. Consider a point mass <math>m</math> at distance <math display="inline">R</math> from a [[point source]] of mass <math display="inline">M</math> which falls radially inward to it. (Crucially, Kepler's Third Law depends only on the [[semi-major axis]] of the orbit, and does not depend on the [[Eccentricity (orbit)|eccentricity]]). A purely [[radial trajectory]] is an example of a degenerate ellipse with an eccentricity of 1 and semi-major axis <math display="inline">R/2.</math> Therefore, the time it would take a body to fall inward, turn around, and return to its original position is the same as the period of a [[circular orbit]] of radius <math display="inline">R/2,</math> by Kepler's Third Law:<math display="block">t_{\text{orbit}}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{G(M+m)}}\left(\tfrac{R}{2}\right)^{3/2}=\frac{\pi R^{3/2}}{\sqrt{2G(M+m)}}.</math>

To see that the semi-major axis is <math display="inline">R/2,</math> we must examine properties of orbits as they become increasingly elliptical. Kepler's First Law states that an orbit is an ellipse with the [[center of mass]] as one focus. In the case of a very small mass falling toward a very large mass <math display="inline">M,</math> the center of mass is <u>within</u> the larger mass.  The focus of an ellipse is increasingly off-center with increasing ellipticity. In the limiting case of a degenerate ellipse with an eccentricity of 1, the largest diameter of the orbit extends from the initial position of the infalling object <math display="inline">R</math> to the point source of mass <math display="inline">M.</math> In other words, the ellipse becomes a line of length <math display="inline">R.</math> The semi-major axis is half the width of the ellipse along the long axis, which in the degenerate case becomes <math display="inline">R/2.</math>

If the free-falling body completed a full orbit, it would begin at distance <math display="inline">R</math> from the point source mass <math>M</math>, fall inward until it reached that point source, then return to its original position.  In real systems, the point source mass isn't truly a point source and the infalling body eventually collides with some surface. Thus, it only completes half the orbit. But the orbit is symmetrical so the free-fall time is half the period.<math display="block">t_{\text{ff}}=t_{\text{orbit}}/2=\pi\frac{(R/2)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{G(M+m)}}=\pi R/2[\tfrac{R/2}{G(M+m)}]^{1/2}</math>(This formula also follows from the [[Free_fall#Inverse-square_law_gravitational_field|formula for the falling time as a function of position]].)

For example, the time for an object in the orbit of the Earth around the Sun with period <math display="inline">P=1</math> year, to fall into the Sun if it were suddenly stopped in orbit, would be:<math display="block">\tfrac{1}{2}\frac{P}{2^{3/2}}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{P}{4}.</math>This amounts to 64.6 days.

===Infall of a spherically-symmetric distribution of mass===
Now, consider a case where the mass <math display="inline">M</math> is not a point mass, but is distributed in a spherically-symmetric distribution about the center, with an average mass density of <math display="inline">\rho</math>,<math display="block"> \rho=\frac{3M}{4\pi R^3},</math>where the volume of a sphere is: <math display="inline"> \frac43\pi R^3.</math> 

Let us assume that the only force acting is gravity. Then, as first demonstrated by [[Isaac Newton|Newton]], and can easily be demonstrated using the [[divergence theorem]], the acceleration of gravity at any given distance <math display="inline">R</math> from the center of the sphere depends only upon the total mass contained within <math display="inline">R.</math> The consequence of this result is that if one imagined breaking the sphere up into a series of concentric shells, each shell would collapse only subsequent to the shells interior to it, and no shells cross during collapse. As a result, the free-fall time of a [[test particle]] at <math>R</math> can be expressed solely in terms of the total mass <math display="inline">M</math> interior to it. In terms of the average density interior to <math display="inline">R,</math> the free-fall time is<ref>[https://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1994sse..book.....K Stellar Structure and Evolution] ''adsabs.harvard.edu'' [[Rudolf Kippenhahn|Kippenhahn, Rudolf]]; Weigert, Alfred. Springer-Verlag, 1994: 3rd ed., p. 257 {{ISBN|3-540-58013-1}}</ref>:<math display="block">t_{\text{ff}}=\tfrac14\sqrt{\tfrac{3\pi}{2G\rho}}\simeq 0.5427\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{G\rho}}\simeq 66430\frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}}</math>where the latter is in [[SI]] units.

This result is exactly the same as from the previous section when <math display="inline">M\gg m.</math>

==Applications==
The free-fall time is a very useful estimate of the relevant timescale for a number of astrophysical processes. To get a sense of its application, we may write:<math display="block">t_{\text{ff}}\simeq\frac{35\,\mbox{min}}{\sqrt{\rho\ (\mbox{g}\cdot\mbox{cm}^{-3})}}</math>Here we have estimated the numerical value for the free-fall time as roughly 35 minutes for a [[Celestial mechanics|celestial body]] of mean density 1 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

=== Comparison ===
For an object falling from infinity in a [[Parabolic trajectory|capture orbit]], the time it takes from a given position to fall to the central point mass is the same as the free-fall time, except for a constant {{nowrap|<math>\tfrac{4}{3\pi}\approx0.424\,.</math>}}
